Case illustrated
Pneumocystis pneumonia with multiple nodules on computed tomography
Saori Ikeda a,*,1,2
, Noriyo Yanagawa b,1
a Department of Internal Medicine, Tokyo Metropolitan Cancer and Infectious Diseases Center Komagome Hospital, Tokyo, Japan
b Department of Radiology, Tokyo Metropolitan Cancer and Infectious Diseases Center, Komagome Hospital, Japan
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Acute myeloid leukemia
Pneumocystis pneumonia
Nodules
A B S T R A C T
As is well known to us that pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) is one of opportunistic infections, there are not so 
many cases that computed tomography (CT) reveals multiple nodules, especially in non-HIV PCP. In this case, a 
47-year-old female with acute myeloid leukemia has developed PCP. Two years prior to this presentation, she 
had undergone hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) and had not experienced any recurrence. CT 
showed multiple nodules and segmental consolidation with subpleural sparing. Considering that it is refractory 
to levofloxacin, that β-d glucan is elevated, that PCP PCR was positive in the analysis of bronchial lavage fluid, 
and that other viral and fungal infections are unlikely, we clinically diagnosed as PCP. Although multiple nodules 
were thought to be atypical for PCP, CT performed 12 days after starting trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole to 
confirm radiological efficacy demonstrated resolution of the nodules as well as consolidation. The significance of 
the present report lies in the fact that PCP should be kept in mind in the differential diagnosis when there are 
multiple nodules detected on CT in post-HSCT patients.
A 47-year-old woman with acute myeloid leukemia presented to the 
emergency department with fever and dyspnea that was refractory to 
levofloxacin. Two years prior to this presentation, she’d undergone 
HSCT.
She’d been taking the immunosuppressants prednisolone (7 mg/day) 
and tacrolimus (0.2 mg/day), and had not experienced any recurrence. 
She had no prophylaxis for opportunistic infections.
CT revealed the new appearance of multiple nodules and segmental 
consolidation with subpleural sparing, which had been absent 1 month 
earlier. Blood tests showed: white blood cell count, 9800/μL; C-reactive 
protein, 37.42 mg/dL; and β-d glucan, 37.4 pg/mL (reference range: 
0.0–20.0 pg/mL). An antigenemia assay for cytomegalovirus (C7-HRP), 
tests for Aspergillus galactomannan antigen, and a rapid polymerase 
chain reaction (PCR) test for respiratory viruses and some bacteria (the 
BIOFIRE® Respiratory Panel 2.1) all returned negative results. A culture 
of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was negative for bacteria, acid-fast 
bacilli or fungi. However, PCR assay for Pneumocystis jirovecii yielded 
a positive result. Based on these findings, PCP was diagnosed [1], and 
trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was administered for 21 days. CT per­
formed 12 days after starting treatment to confirm radiological efficacy 
demonstrated resolution of the nodules (Fig. 1 A, B).
P. jirovecii usually provokes granulomatous inflammation [2]. The 
development of nodular shadows reflects that reaction and is related to 
host factors, particularly immune reconstitution disease and recovery of 
partial immune efficiency [3]. However, these shadows occur in only 
3–5 % of PCP cases, chiefly among patients with human immunodefi­
ciency virus infection [4]. A previous study suggested that nodules may 
develop in HSCT recipients in the course of immune reconstitution 
following relatively strong immunosuppression. The nodules associated 
with PCP are therefore observed more frequently in HSCT recipients 
than in patients without HSCT [3].
The present case demonstrates that PCP should be kept in mind in the 
differential diagnosis for multiple nodules detected on CT in post-HSCT 
patients.
